chief_complaint: persistent dry cough worst at night, spirometry normal
hpi_details: 28-year-old female presents with a persistent dry cough for the past 2 months. The cough is remarkably worse at night, often waking her from sleep, and is triggered by cold air and exercise. Denies heartburn, post-nasal drip, or fever. Spirometry in clinic today is normal.
ideas: She thinks the dry cough is lingering irritation from a bad cold she had two months ago or perhaps an allergy to dust in her apartment.
concerns: She is worried that the nightly coughing spells will keep exhausting her right when she needs to perform well for a major project deadline at work.
expectations: She hopes to receive a prescription for a strong cough syrup or an inhaler so that she can finally sleep through the night.

available_results.value: FEV1 3.02 L (96% predicted), FVC 3.65 L (98% predicted), FEV1/FVC 0.83
available_results.collected_at: Earlier today before the current assessment

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Bronchial Asthma is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Cough-Variant Asthma: Trial of inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) and albuterol, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: persistent dry cough worst at night, spirometry normal
Key HPI features: A 28-year-old female has two months of dry nocturnal cough triggered by cold air and exercise, with normal clinic spirometry and no fever, reflux, or post-nasal drip symptoms.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Cough-Variant Asthma.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Bronchial Asthma.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Vocal cord dysfunction without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Silent chest (absent breath sounds during severe attack).
management_principles: Confirm variable airflow limitation or bronchial hyperresponsiveness when possible and evaluate alternative chronic-cough causes.
If an inhaled treatment trial is clinically appropriate, prescribe it with inhaler teaching, a written action plan, and response review.
Seek emergency care for severe breathlessness, inability to speak full sentences, cyanosis, drowsiness, or a silent chest.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: Chronic inflammatory airway disease characterized by variable expiratory airflow limitation and bronchial hyperresponsiveness.
red_flags: Silent chest (absent breath sounds during severe attack)

must_ask.say: Do you hear a high-pitched whistling sound when you breathe out or feel chest tightness?
Are your coughing and wheezing attacks worse late at night or early in the morning?
Do cold air, exercise, pollen, dust mites, or pet dander trigger your breathlessness?
Do you or your family members have allergic rhinitis, hay fever, or eczema?
Have you tried a rescue inhaler before, and if so, did it relieve the cough or chest tightness?

history.answer: I've had this persistent dry cough for the past two months, and it gets especially bad at night.
The cough has been going on continuously for about two months now.
It started gradually about two months ago without any clear cold or fever, and I have never had a lingering cough like this before.
No, it's completely dry. I haven't coughed up any phlegm or mucus at all.
It is remarkably worse late at night, and it often wakes me up from sleep coughing.
I have bouts of coughing, but there is no whooping gasp when breathing in, and I have never thrown up from coughing.
Cold air and jogging or working out outdoors definitely trigger severe coughing fits.
I haven't noticed any whistling or wheezing sounds, but my chest feels a bit tight during coughing spells.
I don't feel breathless when resting, only briefly winded when I have a bad coughing fit.
No, I haven't had any fever, chills, or sweating.
No, there has never been any blood when I cough.
No, my weight has been completely steady and I don't have night sweats.
No chest pain when breathing or coughing, just slight soreness from coughing repeatedly.
No runny nose, congestion, sneezing, or feeling of mucus dripping down the back of my throat.
No heartburn, sour liquid backing up into my mouth, or frequent throat clearing.
No trouble breathing when lying flat, and my legs have not swollen at all.
I don't take any blood pressure medicines or other prescription drugs.
No, I have never had tuberculosis and haven't had any contact with anyone who has it.
No one around me at home or work has been sick or coughing.
I have never tried an asthma inhaler or any breathing spray for this cough.
I had mild seasonal eye itching during pollen season a couple of years ago, but no eczema or childhood asthma.
I thought this might just be a stubborn chest cold that never cleared up, or maybe an allergy to dust in my apartment.
I'm really worried because the coughing wakes me up every night, and I can't afford to be sleep-deprived with a major deadline coming up at work.
I don't have any chronic illnesses or ongoing medical problems.
I have never had surgery and have never stayed in a hospital.
I am not taking any prescription medications, over-the-counter pills, or supplements.
No, I don't have any known allergies to medicines or foods.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used electronic cigarettes.
I only have a glass of wine socially once or twice a month.
I work indoors as an accountant in an office, and my home is clean with no pets, birds, or mold.
My mother has mild seasonal allergies, but no one in my family has asthma, chronic lung disease, or lung cancer.
My last period was two weeks ago, my cycles are regular, and there is no chance of pregnancy.

exam.finding: Alert, comfortable, and in no acute respiratory distress.
Blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, pulse 72 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, temperature 36.6 C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Nasal mucosa is pink without swelling; oropharynx is clear without erythema or cobblestoning.
No cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy palpated.
Symmetric chest wall expansion without retractions or localized tenderness.
Normal resonance on percussion across all lung fields bilaterally.
Breath sounds are clear bilaterally with good air entry and no wheezing, crackles, or rhonchi.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal heart sounds and no murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
No digital clubbing, cyanosis, or peripheral edema in the lower extremities.
